subtype: Crying at work and social norms [Regulating]
passage:
Day 1. Vidya's manager tore through her draft in front of the team. Her eyes filled. Raghav, sitting nearby, saw her blink hard, whisper "excuse me" and leave the room. She stood in the stairwell breathing slowly and dabbing her face.

Day 2. Raghav dropped a sticky note on her desk: "That review was harsh. Tea?" She smiled a little.

Day 4. Vidya returned to the manager with three edits marked and said, "I would like to go through your comments point by point." The manager agreed. It was awkward, but she felt steadier.

qa.q: Where did Vidya go after leaving the room?
qa.a: She went to the stairwell.

qa.q: What did Vidya's filling eyes and quick exit suggest, and what else could they mean?
qa.a: They suggested she was hurt or overwhelmed by the harsh feedback, though she might also have been tired. Stepping out let her compose herself.

qa.q: What helped Vidya return to the situation on day 4?
qa.a: She had marked three edits and asked to go through the comments point by point, which gave her a plan.

qa.q: How might Raghav have felt seeing Vidya leave?
qa.a: Raghav probably felt concern and wanted to be kind, since a note offering tea was left the next day.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional tearing up after harsh feedback, stepping out to compose the feelings, and returning with a plan while a peer responds kindly.

subtype: Crying at work and social norms [Regulating]
passage: Elder here, Yusuf. Reena, you asked whether tears at work are shameful. Let me tell you. Early in my career a senior scolded me hard over a client mistake. My eyes filled and my throat tightened. I said, "Give me two minutes," and stepped out to the fire stairs. I breathed in slowly, counted, washed my face. When I came back I said, "Here is how I will fix it," and laid out a plan. The senior said, "Good." Some offices frown on tears, some do not. A colleague, Suresh, left tea on my desk the next day and said nothing. That kindness I remember still. There is no shame, only reading the room.

qa.q: Where did Yusuf go after saying "Give me two minutes"?
qa.a: Yusuf went to the fire stairs.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling when the senior scolded, and how do you know?
qa.a: Yusuf was hurt and overwhelmed, shown by the filling eyes and tight throat. Stepping out was a way to compose the feelings.

qa.q: What steps did Yusuf take that might help someone in the same situation?
qa.a: Yusuf stepped out briefly, breathed slowly, washed the face and returned with a plan to fix the mistake.

qa.q: How might Suresh's tea have felt to Yusuf?
qa.a: It felt like quiet kindness that Yusuf still remembers.

grounding: Elder's story of a young professional tearing up at harsh feedback, stepping out to compose the feelings and returning with a plan, with a peer's kindness.

subtype: Crying at work and social norms [Regulating]
passage: The client would arrive in fifteen minutes, and the manager had just torn into Rukmini's presentation in front of the whole open-plan floor. "Sloppy. Half these numbers don't match. Did you even check?" Rukmini felt her eyes sting and her chin wobble. There was no empty meeting room, no private corner, only rows of desks and people pretending not to look. She picked up her laptop and walked quickly to the stairwell. On the landing the tears came. She let them, pressing her back to the cool wall and breathing out slowly. The door opened; Sangeeta slipped in with a tissue and a bottle of water. "No speeches," she said. "Just this." Rukmini laughed shakily and wiped her face. After a minute she opened the laptop on her knees. "Slide four and slide seven don't match. I can fix both in ten minutes." She walked back in with the corrected deck and her chin steady.

qa.q: Which slides didn't match?
qa.a: Slide four and slide seven.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling after the manager's criticism?
qa.a: Rukmini felt hurt and embarrassed, eyes stinging and chin wobbling, in front of the whole floor with the client about to arrive.

qa.q: How did Rukmini manage the moment?
qa.a: She stepped out to the stairwell, let the tears come and breathed slowly, then returned with a concrete plan to fix the two slides.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta show kindness?
qa.a: Sangeeta followed with a tissue and water, kept it simple with 'no speeches', and gave Rukmini space to recover.

grounding: Shows a young professional tearing up after harsh feedback, stepping out briefly, breathing and returning with a plan, while a peer responds kindly.

subtype: Crying at work and social norms [Regulating]
passage: Arnab had been on the call with the Mumbai client for forty minutes when it happened. "Frankly, this is amateur work," the client said, and hung up. Arnab stared at the black screen. His throat closed, and to his horror his eyes filled. In his first job a senior had told him, "Men don't cry in office." He blinked hard and gripped the desk, but a tear slid down anyway. Baljeet, at the next desk, saw. She didn't comment, and she didn't make a show of looking away. She just said, "Terrace? Five minutes?" Up there, among the water tanks and the neighbouring building's laundry, Arnab let his breath shudder out and wiped his face with his sleeve. "Sorry," he said. "Nothing to be sorry for," Baljeet said. When he had steadied, he said, "Okay. I'll ask for a list of exactly what they want changed, and do it by Friday." They went back down.

qa.q: How long had Arnab been on the call?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling when his eyes filled?
qa.a: Arnab felt hurt by the harsh words and horrified at crying, remembering a senior saying men don't cry in office.

qa.q: What helped Arnab recover and move forward?
qa.a: A short break on the terrace to breathe and wipe his face, then a plan to ask exactly what the client wanted changed and deliver by Friday.

qa.q: How did Baljeet respond, and why was it kind?
qa.a: Baljeet didn't comment or stare, just offered five quiet minutes on the terrace and said there was nothing to be sorry for, letting him recover with dignity.

grounding: Shows a young professional tearing up after harsh words despite workplace norms, stepping out to breathe and returning with a plan, and a peer's kindness.

subtype: Crying at work and social norms [Regulating]
passage:
"...so the report can't go out like this, Naveen. The data section needs to be redone."
Naveen nodded. He opened his mouth to answer and found his eyes had filled. "Sorry. I... sorry."
Dolma pushed the tissue box across the desk. "No need. Take your time."
"I worked all weekend on it." His voice wobbled. "Can I step out for a couple of minutes?"
"Of course. The water cooler's free. Come back when you're ready."
He came back five minutes later, face washed, carrying a notepad.
"Better?" Dolma asked.
"Yes. Thanks. Can we go through exactly what's wrong in the data section? I'd like to fix it by Thursday."
"That's a good plan." She turned her screen toward him. "And Naveen, the structure is strong. It's only the data. I should have said that first."
He let out a breath. "That helps."

qa.q: By when does Naveen want to fix the data section?
qa.a: By Thursday.

qa.q: Why did Naveen's eyes fill up?
qa.a: He felt hurt and disappointed, having worked all weekend on the report, and the criticism hit hard.

qa.q: What did Naveen do that helped him recover?
qa.a: He asked to step out for a few minutes, washed his face, then came back with a notepad and a plan to fix the data by Thursday.

qa.q: What did Dolma realise about how she gave feedback?
qa.a: Dolma realised she should have mentioned the strong structure first, and tried to make up for the harshness by saying it now.

grounding: Shows a young professional tearing up at feedback, stepping out briefly and returning with a plan, and a manager responding with kindness.

subtype: Crying at work and social norms [Regulating]
passage:
The review happened in my second year at the agency. The creative head flipped through my campaign in front of six people and said, "This is lazy. Start over." I felt my eyes fill before I could stop them. I've always hated that about myself.
I said, "Give me two minutes," and walked to the stairwell. I cried properly there, maybe for five minutes, then washed my face and breathed until my hands were steady.
Sumit came down with a paper cup of water. He didn't say "don't cry" or "that's just how the boss is." He just asked, "Want company, or want to be alone?" I said company.
When I went back up, I asked the creative head for ten minutes to go through what exactly wasn't working. I came out with a list, not just a wound. I'm Trisha, and that's what I'd tell anyone now: step out, then come back with a plan.

qa.q: What did the creative head say about the campaign?
qa.a: "This is lazy. Start over."

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling when the tears came in the meeting?
qa.a: Trisha felt hurt and ashamed after harsh criticism in front of six people, and frustrated at not being able to stop the tears.

qa.q: What steps helped Trisha recover and move forward?
qa.a: Stepping out to the stairwell, letting the tears come, washing up and breathing, then going back to ask for specific feedback and leaving with a list.

qa.q: How did Sumit see the tears, judging by what he did?
qa.a: He seemed to see them as a normal reaction to a hard moment, so he brought water and asked whether Trisha wanted company, without telling Trisha to stop.

grounding: A young professional tears up after harsh feedback, steps out briefly to breathe, returns with a plan, and a peer responds with kindness.
